evals.prompt: Define research synthesis in 2-3 sentences. Name what it operates on and what it produces.
expected_elements: Operates on a corpus of raw qualitative material (transcripts, field notes, diary entries, observation logs)
Turns it into themes, insights, and design-ready artifacts a team can act on
Names canonical methods: affinity mapping (KJ method), plus empathy maps / JTBD / personas
Distinguishes it from collecting data and from summarizing a single document

evals.prompt: Why does affinity mapping cluster observations bottom-up by proximity and name themes only afterward, rather than sorting into pre-existing categories?
expected_elements: Themes should emerge from the evidence, not be imposed by the researcher
A theme named too early becomes a magnet that pulls unrelated observations into it
Delaying naming (IDEO field guide / d.school) keeps the researcher re-evaluating whether two cards belong together
Bottom-up clustering produces defensible themes rather than impression-based ones

evals.prompt: What is the tension between speed/intuition and traceability in synthesis, and which side does the discipline favor and why?
expected_elements: Fast impression-based summary reproduces the researcher's priors rather than the participants' patterns
The discipline favors slow, physical, traceable synthesis over speed
Every theme must trace back to at least two specific, attributable cards
The cost of speed is unfalsifiable conclusions; the benefit of slowness is defensibility

evals.prompt: You have 14 interview transcripts. Walk through how you would synthesize them into a small set of insight statements.
expected_elements: Download research first: lift atomic observations onto a shared surface, one observation per card, in the participant's words
Cluster bottom-up by proximity into emergent themes; name clusters only when their shape is undeniable
Move from descriptive themes (what we heard) to insights (what it means) to point-of-view statements
Produce a small set (typically 3-7) of insight statements in observation + interpretation + implication form

evals.prompt: Describe the three layers of synthesis output (themes, insights, point-of-view statements) and what each requires from the layer below it.
expected_elements: Descriptive themes = what we heard; built from clustered cards
Interpretive insights = what it means; built on top of themes
Point-of-view statements = what we will act on; built on insights
Each layer requires the previous one as evidence — they are not collapsed into one bullet list

evals.prompt: A teammate hands you a single PDF report and asks you to 'synthesize' it, and separately asks you to run five more interviews. Are either of these research-synthesis work? Why or why not?
expected_elements: Summarizing a single document is NOT synthesis — synthesis is built for cross-session pattern extraction across a corpus
Running new interviews is NOT synthesis — that is user-research (collecting primary data)
Correctly distinguishes transforming a corpus from collecting data and from document summarization
Notes user-research and research-synthesis are needed in that order

evals.prompt: A researcher says 'I read all the transcripts, I get the gist — users want simplicity.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: The 'gist' is the danger — a comfortable label named too early pulls unrelated observations into it
Impression-based summary reproduces the team's priors, not the participants' patterns; it is unfalsifiable
Real synthesis is slow, physical, delays naming, and traces every theme to specific cards
Good synthesis should surface at least one uncomfortable, belief-contradicting insight

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a synthesis was done well rather than charitably reproducing prior assumptions?
expected_elements: Every theme traces back to at least two specific cards, each attributable to a session/participant
Themes were named after clusters formed, not before
At least one insight contradicts a prior team belief
Output distinguishes observations / interpretations / implications and is small enough to act on (typically 3-7 themes)
A reader unfamiliar with the raw research could roughly predict what a participant said (specificity is preserved)
